note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; code is spelled the way it is said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: Every bound so far priced a single run. But a data structure is used again and again, so ask about the whole sequence.
A vector takes a million appends. Exactly one of them copies more than half a million keys, and yet people say append is constant time.
These two statements do not contradict each other, and the rest of this reel is why.
One housekeeping choice first. From here a unit of cost is one element written to memory.
The vector doubles its capacity whenever it is full, copying every key across.
Count one unit for each key you add and one for each key you copy.
Now add up the bill for all million appends. What do they cost together?
answer: About two million. Exactly, two million, forty eight thousand, five hundred seventy five.
A million units for the new keys, plus roughly a million for the copies, which come in the sizes one, two, four, and so on. Together, under three n.
Compare that with charging every append the price of the worst one: roughly half a trillion units. That is a true upper bound and a useless one.

lines: Here is the rule. An empty vector has capacity zero. The first append allocates one.
An append to a full vector allocates twice the capacity, copies every key, then writes the new one.
Sixteen appends cost one, two, three, one, five, one, one, one, nine... and then seven ones.
Total, thirty one.
This is the aggregate method: bound the total for any n operations, then divide by n.
The writes cost n. The last resize copied under n keys, and each earlier resize copied half as many as the next one.
So the copies form the sum one, two, four, and so on, and that is less than twice its last term. Under two n.
Total: under three n for n appends, so each append is constant time, amortized.
There are now three different kinds of promise, so keep them apart.
Average case averages over inputs. Expected case averages over the algorithm's own coin flips. Amortized does neither, since nothing here is random.
It is a worst case guarantee, but about the total of a whole sequence, then divided by its length.
So from empty, any n appends cost less than three n together, while a single one among them may still cost n.
The accounting method reaches the same bound with a different picture: pay in advance.
Charge every append three units. One pays for writing the key. One stays on the new key as a coin. And one goes onto a key in the older half, which has no coin yet.
When the row fills, every key carries a coin, and a coin is exactly what that key's copy will cost.
So the next doubling is already paid for, one key at a time.
A proof needs more care than the picture. Call the real cost of operation i c sub i, and the charge for it c hat sub i.
The charges must cover the costs after every operation, not merely at the end. Think of a bank balance: charges in, costs out, and it must never dip below zero.
If it does, you have spent money you never collected, and the bound is worth nothing.
Keep it non negative and n operations cost at most three n.
Why does it multiply?
Grow by one slot, and append i copies i minus one keys. So n appends cost about n squared over two. Half a trillion writes, at a million.
A step of a thousand slots divides that by about a thousand... and it is still quadratic.
Growing by a constant factor makes the copies a geometric series, and that sum is linear in n.
Doubling copies at most about two keys for each append.
A growth factor of one point five leaves less empty space after each resize.
At most how many copies can each append cost, on average?
answer: About three.
Just after a resize that copied c keys, all the copies so far add up to about c times g over g minus one. And n is about c.
For doubling that is two. For one point five, it is three.
Add the new key's own cost, and the accounting charge is one plus g over g minus one. Three for doubling, four for one point five.
The space saved: right after a resize, a third of the capacity is empty, not a half.

lines: About g over g minus one is a peak. You come closest to it just after a resize, and never quite reach it.
Just before the next resize, it falls to about one over g minus one.
After a million appends, doubling has copied only about one point zero five keys for each one. Not two.
And one point five has copied about two point one.
So check measurements against the whole curve, not against a single number.
A binary counter, counting up from zero.
An increment turns the trailing ones into zeros, and the next zero into a one. So one increment can flip every bit. The sixteenth flips five.
How many bits do sixteen increments flip in total?
answer: Thirty one.
Bit zero flips on every increment.
Bit one, on every second.
Bit i, on every two to the power of i.
Sixteen plus eight plus four plus two plus one.
For any n, the total is under two n. So, big O of one amortized, against theta of log n for the worst single increment.
And a vector of sixteen appends also costs thirty one. At a power of two, both come to two times n, minus one.

lines: Accounting for the counter. Charge two per increment.
Every increment sets exactly one bit from zero to one. One unit pays for that. The other stays on the bit, as a coin.
A carry resets bits that are ones, and each one has its own coin.
So the coins always equal the number of ones. The bank never goes negative.
Now a stack with push, pop, and multi-pop of k, which removes the top k keys, or all of them if there are fewer.
One unit is one key in or out.
One multipop can cost almost n. So a run of n operations looks like it could cost n squared.
But each key is popped at most once after it is pushed. The total is at most twice the pushes.
Charge a push two, and a pop or multi-pop nothing. Each key carries the coin for its own removal.
Look back at the three methods. They are one idea in three forms.
An expensive operation can happen only after cheap ones that set it up. So each cheap one pays a little extra in advance.
Use the aggregate method when one total covers every sequence. Charge per operation when the operations differ, like a push and a multipop.
And the charges are your choice. Any charges that keep the balance at zero or above prove a bound.
The bound rests on two facts. Expensive operations come only after cheap ones set them up. And there is one history, from the start state.
Add decrement, and a five-bit counter can flip all five bits on every operation.
Or keep a saved snapshot of a full vector, and add to that same snapshot again and again... and every one of those appends duplicates all sixteen keys.
A later chapter returns to this, for persistent structures.
Back to the vector.
It has a million keys.
They wrote about two million elements. Under three n.
When that last big resize arrived, the bank held a coin for every key it copied, and one to spare.
But the spike is still one operation, and a request stuck behind it simply waits. Removing that wait is a different problem.
And a vector that also shrinks has nowhere to keep the coins for its shrink.
Time to try it. A teammate suggests charging two per append instead of three: one unit for the write, and one coin on the new key.
Then run the doubling vector from empty and watch the bank. At which append does it first go negative?
answer: The fifth.
By then the costs total twelve, against ten charged.
The coin on each new key pays for its own copy. But a resize copies the older half too, and those keys hold no coins.
At each power of two the bank is back at plus one, so checking only the end would hide the failure completely.

lines: Prove it. Part two.
With a growth factor of one point five, the last resize before the millionth one copies almost seven hundred thousand keys.
Estimate the total copies after a million appends.
answer: About two point one million.
The copies up to that resize add up to about three times the last one. And none follow it before the millionth append.
On average that is two point one per operation. It sits between the trough of two and the peak of three.

lines: Prove it. Part three.
Someone adds multi-push of k, which pushes k keys in one operation.
Is every stack operation still big O of one, amortized?
answer: No.
A thousand operations, alternating multi-push of a thousand and multi-pop of a thousand, cost a million. A thousand each.
Charging two per key still covers every removal, but a multi-push of k keys is then charged two k. The bound was per key... and an operation that creates k keys at once breaks it per operation.
